nodes.label: @perfscale/exe launcher shim (resolves platform package, execs native binary)
nodes.rationale: Mirrors the esbuild/pnpm layout: one platform package per target installed via optionalDependencies, plus a meta package whose bin is a tiny Node shim, so npm installs only the matching os/cpu binary. Missing artifacts fail the build — a partial platform matrix on npm is considered worse than no publish.

nodes.label: bench workflow (scheduled CI benchmark + regression tracking)

nodes.label: Build & Release workflow (tag-triggered build/publish/reset)
nodes.rationale: Linux builds are static musl binaries so they run on both glibc and musl systems; platform packages are published to npm before the meta package so @perfscale/exe's optionalDependencies are resolvable the moment it lands.

nodes.rationale: Verifies the published artifact (checksum-verified download, lint + run of the SQLite example), not just the source.

nodes.rationale: The driver seam is public (register_pubsub_driver) and an `options` object passes driver-specific tuning through verbatim — that is how the pro build's Kafka/Redis/MQTT drivers take their settings; an unknown driver value fails with the list of registered ones.

nodes.label: boundary suite — VU level where cumulative error rate first reaches the threshold
nodes.rationale: Detection is engine-specific: k6 aborts itself via an abortOnFail threshold, locust is read from --csv-full-history, jmeter from accumulated summary + deltas, the native engine from its periodic [stats] lines. Wrapped locust/jmeter rows are omitted because the wrapper is a pass-through — the boundary is an engine property.
nodes.norm_label: boundary suite — vu level where cumulative error rate first reaches the threshold

nodes.label: k6-compatible uniform metric summary across engines
nodes.rationale: k6 and perfscale's native engine share one end-of-run summary shape (http_reqs / http_req_duration lines), and locust CSV stats plus JMeter's console summary are translated into it, so one parser fits every engine and every engine reports in the same shape.
nodes.norm_label: k6-compatible uniform metric summary across engines

nodes.label: Bounded 512-line log channels
nodes.rationale: Producers block when a consumer stalls, so consumers must drain the receiver concurrently with the run, never after it.

nodes.label: std/thresholds@v1 run-level SLO gates
nodes.rationale: Errors are hard: an unknown metric, empty with, or unparseable expression fails the gate and the run, so a broken gate never silently passes CI.

nodes.label: GraphQL-over-HTTP failure semantics
nodes.rationale: GraphQL errors travel in a 200 OK body, so HTTP status alone is not the verdict: partial data plus errors passes and is counted in graphql_errors.

nodes.label: --allow-remote-import fail-closed gate
nodes.rationale: Import resolution happens before the allow_file_actions/allow_process_actions gates, so a network import in an untrusted config is an SSRF primitive and supply-chain vector; permission must come from the caller, never the document — there is deliberately no YAML field that enables it.

nodes.label: http_req_* request metrics
nodes.rationale: Steps whose duration says nothing about target latency (ws-recv, ws-ping, streams, db, process) deliberately do not feed http_req_duration — they would poison the shared percentiles.

nodes.label: Fixed-size HDR histograms
nodes.rationale: 1us-1h range at two significant figures keeps memory flat no matter how long the soak, at the cost of an error invisible at the printed precision.

nodes.label: Live [stats] lines
nodes.rationale: The histogram is never reset, so cumulative percentiles converge instead of jittering; the lines exist for streaming consumers such as the controlplane.

nodes.label: Summary forwarding (report / perfscale serve)
nodes.rationale: Delivery problems are logged as [report] on stderr and never fail the run itself.

nodes.label: Native load profiles (fixed / stages / arrival-rate)
nodes.rationale: Arrival-rate is an open model: new iterations start on schedule even when the system under test slows down, where a closed VU-loop would stretch.

nodes.label: before:/after: run lifecycle
nodes.rationale: before: is fail-fast because a broken setup would make every iteration fail identically; after: is best-effort and runs on every exit path because partial cleanup beats none.

nodes.label: Run-scoped managed process registry and auto-kill
nodes.rationale: A forgotten kill_process never leaks a server: whatever is still alive when the run ends is stopped automatically (SIGTERM escalated to SIGKILL, whole process group).
nodes.norm_label: run-scoped managed process registry and auto-kill

nodes.label: Two-stage SIGINT/SIGTERM handling
nodes.rationale: The second signal exits immediately with exit(130) because teardown itself may be wedged and the operator clearly wants out.

nodes.label: ws_msg_rtt application-level message RTT
nodes.rationale: Waiting on a server-push stream is deliberately not counted as latency — how long a server chooses to wait before pushing is not target latency.

nodes.label: perfscale CLI install and first run
nodes.norm_label: perfscale cli install and first run

nodes.label: ${{ }} output interpolation
nodes.rationale: A missing variable resolves to an empty string rather than failing the run; steps without ${{ skip the interpolation pass entirely, so plain steps pay zero overhead.

nodes.label: One-time before: setup with exported outputs
nodes.norm_label: one-time before: setup with exported outputs

nodes.label: Test definition schema as the SDK wire contract
nodes.author: Perfscale Team
nodes.rationale: The YAML/JSON test definition and summary export are chosen as the SDK's true cross-language wire contract rather than any Rust type: schemas, a validator (perfscale lint), an idempotent execution endpoint, and SummaryExport already exist. Additive-only versioning with a schemaVersion rejection gate is required because lenient parsing can silently produce wrong load tests (e.g. ignored multipart field sends an empty-body POST that looks green).
nodes.norm_label: test definition schema as the sdk wire contract

nodes.label: perfscale facade crate with curated re-exports
nodes.author: Perfscale Team
nodes.rationale: Chosen over stabilizing perfscale-core directly: the facade costs one more crate and re-export boilerplate but buys freedom to keep refactoring engine internals while downstreams (perfscaled, currently on git-main and broken twice in one week by signature changes) pin a semver surface. Engine global state (OnceLock clients/caches) and tokio runtime ownership must be scoped or documented before 1.0.
nodes.norm_label: perfscale facade crate with curated re-exports

nodes.label: Thin language SDKs (builders + drivers, not engines)
nodes.author: Perfscale Team
nodes.rationale: JS/Python SDKs build schema-valid definitions and drive execution via CLI subprocess or agent HTTP instead of FFI/napi/pyo3 bindings: load generation is not latency-sensitive on the control path, so a subprocess launch is noise against a 30s test, while bindings would multiply the build matrix by platforms x runtime versions. Data types are generated from the JSON Schema; builder sugar is handwritten on top.
nodes.norm_label: thin language sdks (builders + drivers, not engines)

nodes.label: Composition actions (parameterized step bundles)
nodes.author: Perfscale Team
nodes.rationale: Chosen as the first marketplace execution mechanism: an action expands to existing built-in steps, giving zero new execution surface, zero sandbox problem, and no arbitrary code — value ships in weeks before any WASM investment. Cannot express new behavior (no gRPC via composition), so WASM remains the code-action target once a concrete need justifies the sandbox work.

nodes.label: WASM component actions with capability model
nodes.author: Perfscale Team
nodes.rationale: The credible answer for third-party code actions: wasmtime sandbox, narrow host API, declared capabilities (net, read-file) enforced by the engine. Deferred because sandboxing untrusted code in a load generator is a permanent security commitment (botnet-weaponization risk, metrics-integrity risk, per-iteration cost compounding, and WASM's inability to hold the engine's keep-alive connection pool).
nodes.norm_label: wasm component actions with capability model

nodes.label: MinIO-backed static registry with lockfile pinning
nodes.author: Perfscale Team
nodes.rationale: Chosen over building a real package registry: MinIO already serves the agent binary with anonymous download and sha256 verification, so a static JSON index plus artifacts keyed by marketplace/<publisher>/<name>/<version> yields a cheap MVP. Explicit perfscale install + perfscale.lock (version + digest) is chosen over implicit run-time fetch, which would be a remote-code-execution footgun; run time stays offline against the cache.
nodes.norm_label: minio-backed static registry with lockfile pinning

nodes.label: Child-context scoping for composite steps
nodes.author: Perfscale Team
nodes.rationale: A composite runs in a child context where only inputs.* and its own step outputs are visible, and the caller sees only the declared outputs — the opposite of a textual macro. Chosen despite extra plumbing because the black-box contract (no state capture, no reliance on internals) is precisely the property that makes marketplace-shared composites safe, which RFC 002 phase 1 depends on.

nodes.label: Teardown-always guarantee with cooperative cancellation
nodes.author: Perfscale Team
nodes.rationale: Teardown must run on normal completion, load-phase error, and SIGINT/SIGTERM — chosen over teardown-on-success-only because cleanup after a failed run is exactly when it is needed. This drags in a signal handler, cooperative VU cancellation, a run-once latch (end-of-duration and Ctrl-C can race), and a bounded teardown timeout; SIGKILL/OOM honestly break the promise and must be documented bluntly.

nodes.label: UPCOMING.md release-notes workflow
nodes.rationale: Entries are appended below an HTML comment as features land; on a v* tag the release workflow publishes everything below the comment as the release body (with the auto-generated changelog appended) and resets the file to the template. Empty file at tag time falls back to auto-generated notes with a warning.

nodes.label: CI pipeline integration
nodes.rationale: perfscale runs headless by design so it drops straight into CI: run summary to stdout, exit code gates the job, --summary-export writes machine-readable JSON or a Markdown table for downstream steps.

nodes.label: perfscale CI exit codes
nodes.rationale: 0 = run completed (individual failed requests/checks do not change that — gate on summary.json instead), 1 = run could not execute, 2 = invalid arguments. Deliberate exception: a std/thresholds@v1 gate violated at severity fail fails the process after the summary export, so CI turns red on SLO breaches.

nodes.label: Step interpolation (${{ }} placeholders and ${} generator tokens)
nodes.rationale: ${{ }} resolves once before the action runs while single-brace ${} tokens expand per execution/send; unknown names resolve to empty string and an unterminated ${{ is left as-is.
nodes.norm_label: step interpolation (${{ }} placeholders and ${} generator tokens)

nodes.label: memory pubsub driver (in-process broadcast bus)
nodes.rationale: One channel per subject shared by all VUs — cross-VU fan-out is a feature, not leakage. Needs no broker: fastest way to build test logic and shows the engine's raw ceiling; diffing against a real broker driver isolates what the broker costs.

nodes.label: nats pubsub driver (core NATS via async-nats)
nodes.rationale: Core NATS only: no JetStream persistence, streams, or queue groups — a subscriber not yet connected misses messages, so the step subscribes first to keep same-step roundtrips safe.
nodes.norm_label: nats pubsub driver (core nats via async-nats)

nodes.label: Pro vendor drivers (Kafka, Redis, MQTT)
nodes.rationale: Vendor drivers are a pro capability registered on the same driver seam; their tuning travels in the step's options object, and an unknown driver value fails the step listing registered drivers so it is always clear which build you are running.

nodes.label: Upcoming fix: perfscale lint accepts gpu: configs
nodes.norm_label: upcoming fix: perfscale lint accepts gpu: configs

nodes.label: Upcoming: ${{ env.NAME }} interpolation
nodes.rationale: env.* fails the step on a missing variable instead of silently sending an empty credential; resolved values are substituted into parameters only and never written to logs or summaries, making env.* the right channel for secrets.

nodes.label: Stepped ramping-VU profile (closed model)
nodes.rationale: Closed model: each plateau is a measurement point — periodic [stats] lines share a timeline with the GPU timeseries, showing how tok/s and TTFT degrade as concurrency grows.

nodes.label: Arrival-rate profile (open model)
nodes.rationale: Open model: new requests arrive on schedule even when the server is behind; the rate where TTFT climbs and dropped_iterations first grows past 0 is the practical capacity for this model/prompt.

nodes.label: GPU bench results layout and summary table
nodes.norm_label: gpu bench results layout and summary table

nodes.label: arrival.yaml arrival-rate profile config
nodes.rationale: Open model: completion rate steps up every minute while the engine scales a worker pool; a permit arriving while all max_vus workers are busy is dropped and counted in dropped_iterations — that rate is the server's practical capacity.

nodes.label: stages.yaml stepped ramping-VU profile config
nodes.rationale: Closed model: each plateau raises concurrency so the run shows where tokens/sec flattens and TTFT starts climbing as the model server saturates the GPU; [stats] lines and the gpu timeseries share a timeline so each hold level maps to its own measurement window.

nodes.label: scripts/bench.sh engine comparison benchmark
nodes.rationale: Every scenario hits the same perfscale serve instance on loopback so any gap between a perfscale row and its native counterpart is perfscale's wrapping overhead, not the underlying tool; fixed-duration wall time is misleading, so throughput numbers are where engines actually differ.

nodes.label: ActionHandler registration seam for downstream crates
nodes.rationale: Proprietary actions (e.g. pro/fix@v1) plug in without a fork by implementing the ActionHandler trait and calling register_action; registered handlers are consulted only for IDs no built-in std/* action matches, so built-ins pay no lookup cost.
nodes.norm_label: actionhandler registration seam for downstream crates

nodes.label: gpu::GpuCollector extension seam
nodes.rationale: perfscale-core exposes gpu::GpuCollector and gpu::register_gpu_collector so a downstream build can register richer collectors (NVML, rocm-smi, powermetrics) or shadow the built-ins; the basic metrics are the OSS baseline every collector reports.

nodes.label: Request metrics (http_req_*)
nodes.rationale: Steps whose duration says nothing about target latency (ws-recv, ws-ping, grpc streams, db steps, process actions) deliberately do not feed http_req_duration, because that would poison the shared percentiles.

nodes.label: Failure-rate metrics (<family>_failed)
nodes.rationale: One 0/1 sample is recorded per invocation (not per duration sample), so failed/total is exactly the step family's failure rate — which is what std/thresholds@v1 evaluates with rate.

nodes.label: Variables and ${{ ... }} interpolation
nodes.rationale: A missing stored variable resolves to an empty string, but ${{ env.NAME }} with NAME unset fails the step before the action runs — a silently empty api_key would surface as a confusing 401; env values never reach logs or summaries.

nodes.label: Composing documents with import:
nodes.rationale: Remote imports are fail-closed behind --allow-remote-import because import resolution happens before the allow_file_actions/allow_process_actions gates — a remote base could otherwise grant itself those rights; a document can never opt itself into the network.

nodes.label: std/llm@v1 metrics-returning observer seam (release note)
nodes.rationale: User-facing framing of the change: downstream pro builds merge extra per-request metrics (ITL/TPOT percentiles, cost) into the step's metrics object under their own keys; engine llm_* keys win collisions and observer panics stay contained.

nodes.label: GPU samples carry pro extras (release note)
nodes.rationale: User-facing framing: GpuSample.extra (flattened in JSON) lets collectors registered via register_gpu_collector attach their own numeric fields — clocks, throttle bitmasks, per-process aggregates — to the run summary's GPU timeseries.
nodes.norm_label: gpu samples carry pro extras (release note)

nodes.label: Issue #12 — streaming reporters release
nodes.rationale: Release-notes entry naming the streaming-reporters feature (issue #12): report.reporters streams to std/report/serve@v1, std/report/prometheus-rw@v1 and std/report/otel@v1 with engine-owned keys, label merge, bounded queues, retries and final flush; max_samples moved out of with: (legacy key still reads).

nodes.label: Streaming reporters (report.reporters, issue #12)
nodes.rationale: report.reporters can stream live cumulative metrics during the run to pluggable sinks, generalizing the historical report.url path; engine-owned keys (during_run, interval_ms, labels, max_series) sit next to use: while with: holds reporter-owned parameters. Lets perfscale stand in for k6 -o experimental-prometheus-rw with live Grafana dashboards.

nodes.label: std/report/serve@v1 reporter
nodes.rationale: The perfscale serve sink exposed as a reporter; the legacy report.url + during_run spelling still works and maps to this reporter. POSTs {samples, seq} batches to <url>/api/v1/metrics.

nodes.label: std/report/prometheus-rw@v1 reporter
nodes.rationale: Prometheus remote write sink using Snappy + protobuf; with.url targets the remote write endpoint; with.histogram selects classic (_bucket{le}) histograms (default, works everywhere) or native histograms (opt-in, backend feature required).

nodes.label: std/report/otel@v1 reporter
nodes.rationale: OTLP/gRPC sink (with.endpoint, e.g. an OpenTelemetry collector on :4317); exports exponential histograms with cumulative temporality and run start as start_time_unix_nano; counters/rates become monotonic cumulative sums, gauges stay gauges.

nodes.label: Bounded drop-oldest queue / backpressure policy
nodes.rationale: Each reporter has an independent bounded queue (with.max_pending, default 24); overflow drops the OLDEST snapshot/batch counted in perfscale_report_dropped_snapshots_total{reporter}. The engine never blocks on streaming: snapshots go over a bounded channel with try_send, so a slow or dead backend can never block the VUs, another reporter, or fail the run. Drop accounting is idempotent per run.

nodes.label: Batched delivery (with.batch_size)
nodes.rationale: Reporters batch by with.batch_size (default the run-level report.batch_size, 500); batches never exceed the batch size — an oversized snapshot splits into sequential batches, in order. One snapshot pump feeds all reporters at the fastest requested interval.

nodes.label: Retry with exponential backoff (with.retry)
nodes.rationale: Transient failures retry the same batch with exponential backoff (with.retry: max_attempts x backoff range like 1s..30s; Retry-After hint honored): network errors, HTTP 429/5xx, and transient gRPC statuses (Unavailable, ResourceExhausted, DeadlineExceeded). Any other 4xx or gRPC status is poison — dropped with a warning, never retried.

nodes.label: Synchronous final flush (with.final_timeout)
nodes.rationale: At run end the engine emits one terminal cumulative snapshot and the backlog coalesces to it — older batches are strict cumulative prefixes, so only the terminal snapshot is delivered. The flush is synchronous, bounded by with.final_timeout (default 30s); the CLI waits for it, and a failed or timed-out flush warns but never fails the load run.

nodes.label: Label merge: step > reporter > run
nodes.rationale: Labels come from three levels merged with priority step > reporter > run; values are scalars with ${{ inputs.* }} / ${{ env.* }} interpolation resolved once before the run. run_id and worker (shard index) are engine-set and rejected in user config; a step's own labels: apply only to that step's metrics.

nodes.label: Cardinality guard (max_series)
nodes.rationale: max_series (default 10000) caps each reporter's output series, classic buckets included; series beyond the limit are dropped deterministically (sorted order) and counted in perfscale_report_dropped_series_total{reporter}; the run continues. The report family's own counters are exempt.

nodes.label: report metric family (perfscale_report_*_total)
nodes.rationale: Per-run delivery counters (isolated across concurrent runs) registered as the report metric family — perfscale_report_dropped_series / _dropped_snapshots / _errors — exported to each backend as ..._total{reporter="<use>"} riding the snapshots; the terminal flush refreshes them before final export; also folded into the report@v1 document and summarized on stderr.

nodes.label: Bucketed histogram export, no client-side quantiles
nodes.rationale: Histograms stream bucketed, never as client-side quantiles, because quantiles from N workers cannot be merged while buckets can; backends compute correct cross-worker quantiles, e.g. histogram_quantile(0.95, sum by (le) (rate(http_req_duration_bucket[1m]))). Durations export in seconds.
nodes.norm_label: bucketed histogram export, no client-side quantiles

nodes.label: Cumulative snapshot model
nodes.rationale: All streamed values are cumulative since run start (HDR histograms and counters never reset), so a dropped snapshot only costs time resolution — the next snapshot restores every counter and histogram; consumers diff successive snapshots for per-window numbers. Snapshots carry {samples, seq} with a monotonically increasing seq reused across retries for dedup.

nodes.label: Platform/agent authenticated streaming
nodes.rationale: The CLI ships unauthenticated; the machine agent runs the same shipper with a Keycloak/machine token, stamping every sample with task_id and machine_id, feeding the run page, Metrics dashboard, Prometheus-compatible query API (/api/v1/integrations/prometheus) and Remote Write into the user's own Prometheus/Mimir.

nodes.label: Final-only reporters (json/junit/html/wasm)
nodes.rationale: std/report/json@v1, std/report/junit@v1, std/report/html@v1 and WASM reporters are final-only: during_run: true on them is a lint/run error, not a silent no-op; streaming delivery knobs in with: are rejected on final-only reporters.

nodes.label: PubSubOutcome.errors field (code counterpart)
nodes.rationale: INFERRED: the docs describe the output metrics object carrying pubsub_errors which 'adds the synchronous failure flag to driver-reported asynchronous failures, so it can exceed 1 per exchange' — this is the documented surface of the PubSubOutcome.errors counter in the step implementation; the struct name itself is not named in the docs.

nodes.label: scope semantics (exchange vs vu)
nodes.rationale: scope: exchange (default) opens a fresh broker connection per exchange with connect cost visible in pubsub_connect_ms; scope: vu keeps one warm connection per VU reused across exchanges — only the first exchange per VU pays connect. Broker drivers only; memory ignores scope.

nodes.label: pubsub_errors metric
nodes.rationale: Counter emitted on every exchange: the synchronous failure flag (connect failure, publish error, subscribe shortfall) plus driver-reported asynchronous failures (Kafka delivery errors with flush: none, MQTT ack timeouts, Redis pipeline error replies). 0 on success (the db_errors convention), can exceed 1 per exchange; asynchronous errors are counted without failing the step.

nodes.label: pubsub metric family (msgs_published/msgs_received/publish_ms/connect_ms/e2e_ms/e2e_ms_failed)
nodes.rationale: Per-exchange custom metrics: pubsub_msgs_published/pubsub_msgs_received counters, pubsub_publish_ms and pubsub_connect_ms and pubsub_e2e_ms HDR histograms, derived pubsub_e2e_ms_failed failure rate; gateable via std/thresholds@v1.

nodes.label: pubsub bench suite
nodes.rationale: Bench suite driving one fixed ~256-byte message per iteration against a real NATS broker (BENCH_NATS_URL): cold rows under scope: exchange, warm rows under scope: vu, a warm flush=none fire-and-forget row matching the k6 xk6-nats posture, and pub/sub e2e rows waiting on a per-VU subject; k6 rows use a custom xk6-nats binary and have no measurable e2e row.

nodes.label: specjbb suite (SPECjbb2015, opt-in)
nodes.rationale: Opt-in suite (never in the default list or CI default) running the commercial SPECjbb2015 Java benchmark via SPECJBB_HOME/SPECJBB_JAR; reports native max-jOPS and critical-jOPS (Java operations/s — explicitly NOT HTTP RPS and not comparable with engine tables) plus mode, duration, CPU and peak RSS; invalid kit path fails the bench, never a fake success.

nodes.label: renaissance suite (Renaissance MIT)
nodes.rationale: Suite running the Renaissance benchmark suite's MIT distribution (JVM workloads, default finagle-http, pinned sha256-verified renaissance-mit-0.16.2.jar); part of the default suite list and daily CI; reports operation throughput in ops/s (NOT HTTP RPS) and per-operation time (mean/min/max ms) plus repetitions, duration, CPU and peak RSS; rows never join the engine comparison tables.
